proposed.text: Architect A created a distinctive hotel design with a unique curved facade and innovative interior spatial flow. Architect B, without authorization, created a new building with an identical curved facade and nearly identical interior spatial arrangement. Can Architect A pursue infringement remedies under RA 8293?

options.text: No, because buildings are functional structures that cannot be protected by copyright, unless they contain significant artistic elements
Yes, if Architect A can prove Architect B copied the specific creative expression, not merely the functional concept
Only if Architect A had registered the design with IPOPHL before Architect B's work began, ensuring legal protection under intellectual property laws
No, because the functional building code requirements make the design inherently non-protected, unless it can be shown to have artistic merit

rationale.a: Buildings and architectural works are expressly included in RA 8293; the functional nature of a building does not remove all protection.
rationale.c: RA 8293 Section 172.2 protects works by the sole fact of creation; registration is not stated as a condition for copyright to exist.
rationale.d: Functional or code-required similarities are not enough, but distinctive copied expression can be protected.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 protects works of architecture and plans or three-dimensional works relative to architecture, but Section 175 excludes ideas, systems, methods, concepts, principles, and mere data as such. Section 186 specifically covers erection of a building reproducing the whole or a substantial part of a protected architectural work. The claim depends on copying protected expression, not merely using the same functional concept.
rationale.takeaway: Architectural copyright analysis asks whether protected expression was copied, not whether the buildings share a generic function.
